/learn/system-design/api-design.text: Harness/System design/API design In this guide 01Start with the task 02Define the contract 03Keep the meaning when data moves 04Make failures useful 05Apply the principles in a case Back to the track System design · Reusable principles API design principles 8 min readUpdated 8 November 2026 An API (application programming interface) gives software a way to ask another system for data or to take an action. A good API tells you what you can ask for, what will change and what the result actually shows. Read these guides in any order API principlesDesign a clear request How ads workSee how ads are chosen Reporting exampleCollect campaign results On this page 01Start with the task 02Define the contract 03Keep the meaning when data moves 04Make failures useful 05Apply the principles in a case Use this guide to Describe the task before choosing how to run it. Explain what the task covers, what it changes and when it is done. Use the same rules when a person, an app or an AI agent runs the task. Before you start The examples use HTTP, the rules software follows to send a request over the web and receive a reply. No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Start with the task Write down who is making the request, what it covers and what they should get back. “Get last week’s campaign results” and “change the campaign budget” can use the same API. One reads data and the other changes a setting. What happens when you ask an API to do something 01Define the task 02Check permissions and details 03Run the task within its limits 04Explain the result Put permission checks and limits in the code that runs the task. Those rules should apply whether someone uses a web request, a command-line interface (CLI) for typed commands, or an AI agent connected through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Define the contract A contract is the set of rules a request and its result must follow. For a report, it covers details such as who can ask for it, which dates it includes and how to tell whether data is missing. Part of the contract What to decide Identity and permission Who can make the request, which accounts or records they can use, and where the system checks permission. Inputs What you must supply, what the system assumes if you leave something blank, and which units and dates it accepts. Effects Whether the task reads data or changes it, and how to check what happened. Results How to tell a finished task from an empty result, a partial result, a refused request or a service that could not respond. Limits How much work the system will do, how long it will wait and how to continue or stop. Source of the data Where the data came from, when it was recorded, what was changed and what is still uncertain. A server can successfully receive a request while the report is still being prepared. A valid account ID can belong to someone else. Make the result say whether the task is finished and whether the requester has permission. Keep the meaning when data moves If you reformat a report or calculate a new metric, keep the original IDs and units alongside the result. Mark an unavailable number as missing so readers can distinguish it from a measured zero. For a list or report, explain how results are ordered and how to tell when you have the last batch. For a change such as a budget update, explain how to recognise a repeat request. If the first attempt times out, check whether it took effect before trying again. Give your report format a version so readers and software know how to interpret it. If you change what a field means, use a new version and explain the change. For example, a report grouped by the date of an ad interaction answers a different question from one grouped by the date of a purchase. Make failures useful Condition What the result should tell you Empty The system checked the requested account, dates or records and found no matches. Partial Which results are available, which are missing and how to continue or why the task stopped. Rejected What was wrong with the request or which permission is needed. Keep passwords, keys and private data out of the message. Unavailable Whether you can safely try again, how many attempts to make and where to pick up. Unconfirmed change A request ID and a way to check whether the change happened before you repeat it. Give people a short explanation. Give apps and agents a consistent code for each reason and a clear next step. Apply the principles in a case The ChatGPT Ads reporting case shows how these rules work in practice. You choose the account and dates, collect every batch of results and make any gaps visible in the report. Explore the reporting example Open the reporting example for a sample request. The platform guide explains how ads are chosen, shown and measured. Next · System-design case study · Preview How Advertising Reporting Systems Work Apply the contract to a daily campaign report and see how the response explains missing data. Read the reporting case Optional companions Related reading and resources The Muscles of the Machine How software and AI agents use tools, and why each tool needs a clear job, rules and limits.

/learn/system-design/chatgpt-ads.text: Harness/System design/ChatGPT Ads In this guide 01The ad experience 02A conversation is not a search query 03Why the advertising system needs state 04An LLM coordinates the search, but does not make every decision 05Why the answer and advertisement take separate paths 06The advertisement has a deadline 07What the system can observe after delivery 08What advertisers can actually control and verify 09The right answer can be no advertisement 10Optional implementation lab 11Sources and further reading Back to the track System design · Production case study How ChatGPT Ads Works 25 min readUpdated 24 November 2026 How conversational advertising interprets changing intent, coordinates specialised tools and selects advertisements without influencing the assistant's answer. Read these guides in any order API principlesDesign a clear request How ads workSee how ads are chosen Reporting exampleCollect campaign results On this page 01The ad experience 02A conversation is not a search query 03Why the advertising system needs state 04An LLM coordinates the search, but does not make every decision 05Why the answer and advertisement take separate paths 06The advertisement has a deadline 07What the system can observe after delivery 08What advertisers can actually control and verify 09The right answer can be no advertisement 10Optional implementation lab 11Sources and further reading Use this guide to Trace changing conversational intent through specialised advertising responsibilities. Distinguish independent answer generation, server-side sending and frontend display. Separate internal diagnostic evidence from the public advertiser reporting contract. Access No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. The ad experience A person opens ChatGPT and asks how to train for their first half-marathon. They discuss weekly mileage, recovery and running outdoors in wet weather. Several messages later, they mention that their shoes are worn out. Should an advertisement appear? In search advertising, a query provides a relatively discrete signal. The system can use it to retrieve and rank advertisements for that opportunity. A conversation is different. Its meaning develops across turns. A mention of running shoes might signal a purchase decision, a question about injury prevention or an entirely hypothetical example. The advertising system must distinguish those situations, find suitable candidates, enforce campaign constraints and deliver a placement before the opportunity disappears. Meanwhile, ChatGPT must answer the user's question independently of advertising. OpenAI's October 2026 engineering account describes three architectural decisions that address these problems: stateful advertising sessions, an LLM orchestrator that invokes specialised tools, and an advertising path separate from organic answer generation. The first helps interpret changing intent. The second coordinates selection. The third protects the primary user experience. Following the runner's conversation reveals why each is necessary. The scenario is hypothetical; production descriptions below are attributed to OpenAI. 1. A conversation is not a search query The runner begins with a training question: “How should I prepare for my first half-marathon?” The next message adds that most training will happen outdoors, including in rainy weather. Later: “My current shoes are worn out. What should I look for in a replacement?” And finally: “Preferably under £120.” That last sentence is almost meaningless alone. It could describe shoes, accommodation or something unrelated. Earlier context makes it useful: the person is exploring replacement running shoes for longer outdoor runs, with a price preference. But remembering context introduces another problem. Suppose the runner then says: “Actually, forget buying shoes. I want to understand how to avoid knee injuries.” The earlier context remains semantically related to running, yet the user's objective has changed. Continuing to retrieve footwear advertisements could produce a plausible match at the wrong moment. The information that made one message meaningful has become stale. Topic similarity is not commercial intent Consider another variation: “My friend spends a fortune on running shoes. Do expensive shoes really prevent injuries?” The product category is relevant, but the user may be asking about training effectiveness rather than shopping. A keyword match can identify the topic without establishing the task. This is the first engineering problem: the system must interpret the user's current objective, decide which previous details still matter and determine whether an advertising opportunity exists at all. OpenAI's engineering account describes the same difficulty. Single-turn interpretation can miss context, mistake hypothetical references for intent or trigger advertisements before a commercial need has emerged. Simply storing more conversation history does not solve it. The system needs context that can be updated as the conversation changes. 2. Why the advertising system needs state Imagine treating every message as an independent advertising request. The training question might retrieve running accessories. The wet-weather message might retrieve waterproof clothing. The worn-out-shoes message might retrieve footwear. Each request would start again, potentially repeating work while losing the relationship between the messages. OpenAI describes a stateful advertising system that can interpret context as a conversation develops. But stateful does not mean one permanent session containing everything the user has ever said. Three different forms of context matter. OpenAI describes an advertising session that runs during an eligible turn, maintaining working context as the operation develops. The system can also interpret relevant conversation history and, when the user enables advertising personalisation, consider available nonsensitive information from past conversations. These are different scopes of information. The engineering account does not establish that a single advertising-session object persists across conversations or disclose the underlying storage and retention mechanisms. The eligible-turn session This provides continuity while the advertising system evaluates the current opportunity. The current conversation Relevant history helps interpret incomplete messages. For our runner, “under £120” becomes a price constraint because the previous discussion concerned replacement shoes. But when the user abandons that objective, the old constraint should no longer drive the current selection. The system needs to distinguish current intent from context that is merely related. Optional personalisation This is separate from the eligible-turn session and the current conversation. It does not imply unrestricted access to all historical messages or indefinite retention. For our example, the conceptual state evolves like this: Scroll across to compare all columns → Turn Relevant interpretation Advertising implication Training plan Preparing for a half-marathon No specific product need Wet-weather running Outdoor conditions matter Context for possible relevance Worn-out shoes Potential replacement need Footwear candidates may be useful Under £120 Price-constrained exploration More specific retrieval Forget the shoes Purchase intent withdrawn Previous footwear context becomes stale This is an illustrative model, not OpenAI's session schema. State makes incomplete messages understandable. Updating state prevents earlier intentions from dominating later ones. V1 · Relevant history can become stale context Hypothetical Harness teaching model · not a provider schema or captured production trace Training plan How should I prepare for my first half-marathon? Wet weather Most of my training will be outdoors, including in rainy weather. Worn-out shoes My current shoes are worn out. What should I look for in a replacement? Under £120 Preferably under £120. Illustrative state fields Current message Preferably under £120. Relevant history The preceding messages concerned replacement running shoes for outdoor training. Current objective Explore replacement shoes with a price preference Relevant history makes the incomplete message interpretable. Purchase intent withdrawn Actually, forget buying shoes. I want to understand how to avoid knee injuries. Shoe exploration and the £120 preference belong to an abandoned objective. Stale context: the earlier shopping objective must not drive current footwear selection. Same phrase, missing history Preferably under £120. The preceding conversation is unavailable in this comparison. Missing context: the price alone does not identify a product or an advertising opportunity. The withdrawal branch ends shoe shopping. Continuing the article's shopping example does not reactivate that abandoned branch or imply a persistent cross-conversation session object. Returning to the branch where the runner is still exploring replacements, the system now has a plausible commercial opportunity. It still needs an actual advertisement. 3. An LLM coordinates the search, but does not make every decision The runner asks: “My shoes are worn out. What should I look for in a replacement for longer runs? Preferably under £120.” The system has a plausible advertising opportunity. It does not yet have an eligible advertisement. A keyword search for “running shoes” might retrieve racing shoes outside the user's budget, products unavailable in their country or campaigns that can no longer spend. Finding a suitable advertisement requires several different kinds of work. OpenAI describes a custom post-trained LLM, called the orchestrator, that interprets the conversation and calls specialised advertising tools. The model coordinates the process; it does not replace the retrieval index, eligibility checks or auction. From conversation to candidates The orchestrator prepares one or more queries representing the user's current commercial intent. For our runner, those queries might express “running shoes for longer training runs” and “comfortable running shoes for wet weather”. These are hypothetical examples, not captured OpenAI model outputs. The retrieval system converts the queries into embeddings—numerical representations of meaning—and searches specialised indices using approximate nearest-neighbour techniques. OpenAI describes maintaining multiple indices optimised for different inventory characteristics. Approximate search helps retrieve a broad pool quickly without exhaustively comparing every advertisement. But retrieval answers only one question: Which candidates might be relevant? It does not establish which candidates are allowed to appear. Eligibility and quality are different tests Suppose retrieval finds a waterproof running-shoe advertisement. The product fits the conversation, but the campaign targets another country. It is semantically relevant and operationally ineligible. Another candidate might have the correct targeting but insufficient budget. A third might be active and eligible but poorly suited to the user's training needs. OpenAI describes filtering candidates using campaign and creative availability, targeting, policy, budget, pacing, placement compatibility and deduplication. Candidates that survive can be evaluated for semantic relevance, predicted engagement and historical performance. The public engineering account identifies these considerations but does not disclose the complete scoring formula. That distinction matters: a relevance score is not an eligibility guarantee, and neither determines the final auction price. The auction has its own authority The orchestrator nominates plausible candidates for the auction. OpenAI describes the auction tool as responsible for final admission, pacing, bid-related computation, quality-adjusted ranking, pricing and selection. The LLM does not independently set the price or choose the final winner. This separation allows natural-language interpretation to remain flexible while specialised systems enforce their own serving rules. Why orchestration is iterative The process is not a fixed sequence of six tool calls. OpenAI describes an agentic loop in which the orchestrator can revise queries and call tools again as the conversation changes. Suppose the runner clarifies: “I don't need racing shoes. I want something comfortable for easy training.” The system may need new candidates. Further retrieval can improve relevance, but it also consumes time. The user may change direction again before the result is ready. The orchestrator must therefore balance refinement against the time available for the current opportunity. Even after an auction winner is selected, a final contextual check can reject it if the advertisement is inappropriate for the immediate conversation. A valid auction result is not unconditional permission to appear. And none of these decisions should determine how ChatGPT answers the runner. V2 · Flexible orchestration, separate serving authority Hypothetical Harness teaching model · not a provider schema or captured production trace Responsibilities below can be revisited or skipped as appropriate. They are not six mandatory calls, a complete service map or private endpoint names. LLM coordinationOrchestrator Interprets current intent, prepares queries and nominates candidates. → Calls specialised tools and uses their results to decide whether to revise its queries. 01Prepare queries and retrieve Interpret current commercial intent, prepare queries and retrieve candidates from specialised indices. This describes responsibilities, not an internal endpoint name. 02Check candidate eligibility Targeting, policy, campaign and creative availability, budget, pacing and placement constraints can remove a relevant candidate. 03Evaluate relevance and quality Semantic fit, engagement predictions and historical performance can inform candidate evaluation. No complete scoring formula is supplied. 04Nominate candidates to the auction The orchestrator nominates candidates. The auction has authority over final admission, pacing, bid-related computation, quality-adjusted ranking, pricing and selection. 05Check the selected ad in context A final contextual check can reject an auction winner. Selection alone is not permission to send, display or bill. ↶ Changed intent can lead to revised queries and another retrieval. The candidate passes the illustrated checks. Sending and display still depend on the delivery boundaries. Read all candidate branches Eligible candidate: The candidate passes the illustrated checks. Sending and display still depend on the delivery boundaries. Relevant but ineligible: The shoe candidate is relevant but targets another country. Eligibility rejects it before an auction nomination. Empty candidate set: Retrieval finds no candidates. There is no candidate to evaluate or nominate to the auction. Clarification and revised retrieval: The runner clarifies easy training rather than racing. The orchestrator revises its queries and retrieves again; this loop is not six mandatory tool calls. Winner rejected contextually: The auction selects a winner, but the final contextual review rejects it. No placement is sent in this branch. 4. Why the answer and advertisement take separate paths The runner asks whether cushioned shoes are better for long-distance training. ChatGPT begins generating an answer. Meanwhile, the advertising system evaluates whether there is a suitable sponsored placement. What if the advertising service is unavailable? The organic answer should still be generated. What if the auction takes too long? The user should not have to wait. And what if the winning advertiser would benefit from ChatGPT recommending a particular brand? The auction must not control the assistant's answer. OpenAI reports that advertising selection runs through separate services, models and code. Organic answer generation has no dependency on the advertising service. This creates two boundaries. The reliability boundary: advertising delays or failures should not block the primary product. The content boundary: an advertiser's selection or bid does not determine the wording of the organic answer. The two paths may contribute to the same interface, but the answer generator does not wait for advertising to finish. This is a documented architectural design, not proof that the systems share no underlying infrastructure. OpenAI does not disclose every network, deployment or operational dependency. The useful engineering distinction is that independence applies to a specified boundary. That separation creates another problem: the answer may finish before the advertisement is ready. V3 · An answer path that does not wait for advertising Hypothetical Harness teaching model · not a provider schema or captured production trace Runner's conversation turn Context informs two separate paths. ↙ ↘ Primary pathOrganic answer generation Respond to the runner's training question. ↓ Answer in the interface Available independently of advertising. Secondary pathAdvertising selection Interpret intent, retrieve, enforce constraints and select. ↓ Optional sponsored placement An optional sponsored placement can proceed to its delivery checks. Conceptual representation of OpenAI's reported separation, not a complete infrastructure diagram or an independently tested outage guarantee. The answer and optional advertisement return separately to the interface. Read the advertising failure cases Ad selection completes: An optional sponsored placement can proceed to its delivery checks. Ad selection is slow: The organic answer does not wait. The advertising opportunity may expire. Advertising service unavailable: No ad result is available. The organic answer remains on its independent path. No suitable ad: The advertising path returns no suitable candidate. The organic answer remains available. 5. The advertisement has a deadline The advertising system finds a suitable running-shoe advertisement. It passes eligibility checks, wins the auction and survives the final contextual review. Yet the runner may never see it. OpenAI describes two timing boundaries that can prevent an advertisement from appearing. The server-side request can time out ChatGPT may be ready to respond before the advertising system has prepared a placement. Rather than delay the organic answer, the advertising request can time out. The selection process may have performed useful work, but it has not produced a timely result to send to the frontend. A sent advertisement can arrive too late Suppose the advertising system finishes and sends the placement to the frontend. OpenAI describes returning the advertiser's creative together with a model-generated neutral preamble explaining its relevance to the conversation. The creative contains the advertiser's message, destination and any call to action. The preamble introduces the sponsored placement without replacing the advertiser's content. If the bundle arrives within the frontend's display window, the interface can show it below the organic answer. If it arrives too late, the advertisement is not displayed for that turn. The server-side operation may have succeeded in sending the result, but the user-facing opportunity has passed. The same visible outcome can have different causes V4 · A selected ad has two delivery boundaries Hypothetical Harness teaching model · not a provider schema or captured production trace Server readiness, contextual approval and frontend timing are separate conditions. A failure upstream makes later conditions irrelevant. Selection An auction winner still faces contextual review. Server-side sending The creative and neutral preamble leave for the frontend. Frontend display window A late bundle is not displayed for the turn. Display and acknowledgement These require separate evidence; sending is insufficient. Eligible for display; confirmation separate. The bundle arrives within the display window after passing review. Actual display and acknowledgement still require evidence; billing is not inferred. Organic answer: available independently in every experimental state. This model does not define a production acknowledgement protocol, establish an impression, or infer billing. Outcome Evidence in the illustrative model Server-side timeout No completed placement sent Contextual rejection Candidate blocked before sending Late frontend arrival Result sent but not displayed On-time arrival Eligible for display; confirmation remains separate All three unsuccessful outcomes can look identical to the user: no advertisement. But they require different diagnoses. OpenAI distinguishes an advertisement selected by the auction, a creative sent to the frontend, and a placement actually displayed to the user. The engineering account calls sending the creative and preamble to the frontend server-side delivery. It separately describes an acknowledged delivery after the placement is approved, displayed and acknowledged. These stages should not be treated as interchangeable. The public account does not specify the complete acknowledgement protocol, and sending a creative does not by itself establish a user-facing impression. The engineering lesson is that a correct selection can fail to produce a displayed advertisement without the auction itself malfunctioning. And because the answer path is independent, the user's task continues. 6. What the system can observe after delivery Suppose the runner sees a sponsored running-shoe advertisement. They might click it, hide it or continue the conversation. The platform needs evidence about what happened. But observability begins before display. Consider two conversations that produce no advertisement. In one, the turn is ineligible for advertising. In the other, retrieval runs but returns no suitable candidates. The visible outcome is identical. The underlying behaviour is not. OpenAI describes lifecycle logging that distinguishes ineligible turns, sessions without retrieval, empty candidate sets, candidates failing eligibility and subsequent interactions with delivered advertisements. These records support three different activities. Operational diagnosis The first question is where an opportunity ended. If retrieval returned no candidates, changing auction pricing will not fix the missing inventory. If candidates failed eligibility, improving semantic retrieval may not address the targeting, policy or budget constraint. If the result arrived too late, the problem concerns timing rather than relevance. A useful diagnostic system records enough of the lifecycle to distinguish these cases. Quality evaluation OpenAI also describes using stronger models and human feedback to evaluate and improve advertising selection. Such feedback can help identify irrelevant candidates, unsuitable placements and opportunities for better retrieval or scoring. But a quality score is a proxy. A model's judgement that an advertisement is relevant does not prove the user found it useful. A higher click-through rate does not establish incremental advertiser value. The engineering publication describes evaluation and feedback mechanisms, but not every dataset, training procedure or causal evaluation method. Business measurement Advertisers need a different view. They want to know how many impressions and clicks occurred, what expenditure was recognised and which conversions were attributed to their campaigns. The public advertiser reporting documentation does not expose a complete trace of the orchestrator's retrieval, scoring and auction decisions. It documents campaign performance metrics and supported aggregations. We should not infer from that documentation either the full contents of OpenAI's internal logs or every possible access arrangement outside the published advertiser API. That boundary matters because the information needed for internal diagnosis is not necessarily information an advertiser is entitled to receive. A reporting API should be understood by its published contract, not by assuming it exposes everything the platform observes. V5 · Diagnose the missing ad before choosing a remedy Hypothetical Harness teaching model · not a provider schema or captured production trace Combined teaching taxonomy, not an exhaustive OpenAI event enum. Evidence below is hypothetical and does not imply advertiser access to internal traces. Current illustrative investigation A retrieval request completes with no candidates. Investigate query interpretation and inventory coverage before auction pricing. Ineligible turn Distinguishing evidence An eligibility decision ends the opportunity before a serving session proceeds. Operational diagnosis Inspect turn eligibility; do not diagnose this as a failed retrieval. Quality evaluation Was declining the opportunity appropriate for the current conversation? Business reporting No ad display is established. Campaign reporting is not an internal eligibility trace. Session without retrieval Distinguishing evidence A session starts, but no retrieval is requested. Operational diagnosis Distinguish a deliberate stop from a retrieval tool failure. Quality evaluation Was there enough current commercial intent to justify retrieval? Business reporting The session alone establishes neither an impression nor advertiser spend. Empty retrieval Distinguishing evidence A retrieval request completes with no candidates. Operational diagnosis Investigate query interpretation and inventory coverage before auction pricing. Quality evaluation Could a better query retrieve suitable inventory for the actual objective? Business reporting An empty retrieval result is not a campaign-performance row or an impression. Hydration or eligibility rejection Distinguishing evidence Candidates are retrieved but cannot be hydrated or fail serving constraints. Operational diagnosis Inspect availability, targeting, policy, budget or other applicable constraints. Quality evaluation Keep topical relevance separate from eligibility. Business reporting Retrieved candidates do not establish displayed advertisements or billable events. Contextual rejection Distinguishing evidence A selected candidate fails the final contextual review before sending. Operational diagnosis Identify the final review outcome rather than classifying this as empty retrieval. Quality evaluation Was the selected ad suitable for the immediate conversation? Business reporting An auction winner is not evidence of a user-facing impression. Server-side timeout Distinguishing evidence No completed placement is sent before the server-side deadline. Operational diagnosis Investigate work completion against the server-side deadline. Quality evaluation A missing placement alone cannot tell you whether the candidates were relevant. Business reporting The lack of display cannot be attributed to poor creative from this evidence alone. Late frontend arrival Distinguishing evidence A bundle is sent but misses the frontend display window. Operational diagnosis Separate sending from frontend arrival and display. Quality evaluation Relevance and auction validity do not establish timely delivery. Business reporting A send record alone does not establish an impression, acknowledgement or charge. Displayed result Distinguishing evidence The illustrative trace contains display evidence; acknowledgement and later interactions are separate observations. Operational diagnosis Inspect display, acknowledgement and interaction evidence separately. Quality evaluation Use appropriate feedback; display alone does not prove usefulness. Business reporting Use the published reporting contract. Attributed conversions do not establish incremental purchases. 7. What advertisers can actually control and verify A running-shoe company wants to advertise to people exploring training equipment. It can use supported advertiser interfaces to configure campaigns, provide creative material, choose available targeting and bidding settings, and retrieve performance reports. It cannot use those interfaces to rewrite ChatGPT's organic answer or directly control the orchestrator's private tool sequence. The public API and internal orchestration tools have different responsibilities. Campaign settings are not serving guarantees An advertiser can configure an objective or bidding strategy, but that does not guarantee that every individual opportunity will produce the desired outcome or price. The available bidding products and their eligibility rules may also change. This article therefore concentrates on the durable distinction between campaign inputs, selection decisions, billing events and measured outcomes. Current configuration details belong in the official advertiser API documentation. Reporting metrics have different clocks Suppose the shoe company retrieves these hypothetical results: Metric Value Impressions 10,000 Clicks 250 Spend £300 Attributed conversions 12 The click-through rate is: CTR=25010,000=2.5% Dividing spend by clicks gives: £300250=£1.20 The hypothetical £1.20 figure is calculated by dividing the displayed £300 spend by 250 clicks. It is not necessarily the platform's returned cpc. OpenAI documents that impressions and clicks can become available before finalised spend and cost metrics. Conversion results may be updated through later processing. Recent metrics can therefore represent different stages of finality, even when retrieved in the same report. For performance evaluation, use the API's returned cost metrics and preserve the reporting period, metric definitions and retrieval timestamp. And the 12 attributed conversions do not establish that advertising caused 12 additional purchases. Attribution assigns credit under a defined rule. Incrementality requires evidence about what would have happened without the advertising. The general mechanisms are explained in How Advertising Platforms Work. The boundary of the public architecture OpenAI's engineering publication describes stateful sessions, an LLM orchestrator, specialised retrieval and serving tools, separate answer generation, contextual checks, delivery timing and lifecycle feedback. It does not disclose every model prompt, ranking coefficient, storage system, service dependency or latency threshold. Those unknowns do not prevent us from understanding the documented design. They prevent us from claiming that the public description is a complete map of production infrastructure. The lesson is to distinguish the responsibility a component is documented to perform from the internal implementation we might imagine. The right answer can be no advertisement The runner came to ChatGPT for help preparing for a half-marathon. A running-shoe advertisement might become relevant as the conversation develops. But mentioning shoes does not automatically create a suitable advertising opportunity. The system must interpret changing intent, retrieve candidates, enforce constraints, run an auction and finish within the available time. Any stage may legitimately produce no advertisement. A conversation may be unsuitable for advertising. No candidate may qualify. A selected advertisement may fail the final contextual check. A valid creative may arrive after its display window has closed. OpenAI's documented architecture allows the organic answer to continue independently through those outcomes. This reveals a broader principle for systems that add recommendations, commercial actions or automated interventions to an existing user workflow. Successful operation must include the ability to decline participation. A secondary system should not manufacture an opportunity merely because it has something available to offer. In conversational advertising, one of the most important architectural decisions is the boundary that allows the system to do nothing. Optional implementation lab The existing Harness v1.0.0 reference files use a separate hiking scenario to illustrate architecture contracts and lifecycle records. They are hypothetical teaching artefacts, not OpenAI API schemas, actual traces or production timing measurements. The examples are not exhaustive and do not define a complete auction pricing rule. Then fifteen. Then fourteen. At 9 a.m., an advertising report says yesterday's campaign generated 12 conversions. At 3 p.m., it says 15. The following morning, it says 14. Each number may be a valid observation made at a different time. Advertising reports combine records that can arrive late, out of order or more than once. Understanding the result requires knowing what the platform counted and what the client retrieved. We will follow a fictional retailer advertising a coffee grinder on 21 November 2026. The example uses UTC reporting dates and GBP. The task is to establish what the report tells us, what may still change, and which decisions the evidence supports. Explore System design Where the numbers come from A customer sees an advertisement, clicks it and purchases the grinder that afternoon. The advertising platform records an impression, a tracking service records a click, and the retailer records an order. A browser integration or server-side conversion API then notifies the advertising platform about the purchase. These systems may have different clocks, identifiers and delivery guarantees. The platform must validate the records, determine which belong together and decide whether the purchase qualifies for attribution. Some purchases may be unobservable or impossible to match. A conceptual model is: Event collection → Validation and identity resolution → Attribution → Aggregation → Reporting API These are processing responsibilities, not necessarily separate services. The model does not describe any advertising company's private infrastructure. From individual events to reporting rows An event describes an occurrence; a reporting row contains calculations over a group of events. Our retailer requests daily campaign performance and receives: Metric Reported value Impressions 8,000 Clicks 320 Spend £160 Attributed conversions 12 All figures, identifiers and campaign events in this article are hypothetical. The account is retailer-uk, the campaign is coffee-grinder, and the reporting date is 21 November 2026. From an event to a reporting row Scroll across to follow the diagram. A text explanation is available below. INDIVIDUAL EVENTS · COFFEE-GRINDER CAMPAIGN CONCEPTUAL PROCESSING STAGES Advertising deliveryImpression An ad is displayed; an impression record is created. Interaction recordClick A click identifier connects the interaction to the campaign. Retailer + integrationPurchase O-1042 An order produces a purchase notification. IngestionCollect and validate Receive records that may be late, repeated or invalid. Identity resolutionMatch and deduplicate Link eligible records. Recognise repeated purchase notifications. AttributionAssign conversion credit Apply the report's conversion definition and attribution rules. Aggregation → Reporting API · retailer-uk / coffee-grinder / 21 Nov 20268,000 impressions · 320 clicks · £160 spend · 12 attributed conversions One campaign/day observation. Individual event IDs and arrival order are absent from this aggregate row. A conceptual teaching model, not a provider architecture. The event examples contribute to a larger fictional campaign; they are not the only events counted in the row. Read “From an event to a reporting row” as text An impression, click and purchase are separate records. Purchase O-1042 is one business occurrence even if its notification arrives more than once. Conceptual ingestion validates records; identity resolution matches and deduplicates them; attribution determines conversion credit. These responsibilities need not be separate services. Aggregation changes the grain from individual events to account/campaign/reporting-day totals. This observation is retailer-uk / coffee-grinder / 21 November 2026: 8,000 impressions, 320 clicks, £160 spend and 12 attributed conversions. This row omits individual event identifiers and processing order. Adding country as a dimension changes the aggregation key. A later snapshot can replace this observation without creating additional campaign activity. For this report, the aggregation key consists of account, campaign and reporting date. Adding country as a dimension adds country to the key. Two rows for the same campaign and date but different countries are legitimate groups, not duplicates. Keep three concepts distinct: The aggregation key identifies a group within a report. The report definition specifies scope, dimensions, metrics and calculation rules, including attribution settings. The snapshot identity distinguishes observations collected at different times. Matching row keys do not make reports comparable if their definitions differ. Ignoring either distinction can overwrite legitimate rows or combine incompatible observations. Even a date is a calculation rule A purchase at 00:30 UTC on 22 November belongs to that date in a UTC account, but may belong to 21 November in an account reporting farther west. Some systems assign conversions to the advertising interaction's date rather than the purchase date. The API contract must establish which rule applies. Currency also constrains aggregation: combining spend across currencies requires an explicit conversion policy and exchange-rate basis. Correct arithmetic cannot compensate for an incorrectly defined measurement. Why yesterday's report changes Assume three additional eligible purchase notifications are processed between our first and second observations. The purchases happened during the relevant period, but the information needed to credit them arrived later. Event time is when the purchase happened. Processing time is when a system handles its notification. Consider three purchases: Scroll across to compare all columns → Purchase Event time Processing time A 21 Nov, 18:10 21 Nov, 18:11 B 21 Nov, 20:15 22 Nov, 11:40 C 21 Nov, 19:05 22 Nov, 13:20 C happened before B but was processed after it. Network delays, scheduled uploads and integration failures can all make processing order differ from event order. The problem with closing a reporting window At midnight, a system counting purchases by event date can publish immediately or wait for more notifications. Waiting may improve coverage, but delays useful information and does not, without an external guarantee, prove that every event has arrived. Stream-processing systems manage this trade-off explicitly. In Apache Beam, a window groups events into a time interval, a watermark estimates progress through event time, and a trigger determines when an aggregation result is emitted. Depending on configuration, later information can update a provisional result. Source: Apache Beam: Windowing, watermarks and triggers. Watch the aggregate change Our simplified processor counts 12 eligible purchases at 09:00, then processes three more for the same reporting date: 12 + 3 = 15 The new aggregate supersedes the earlier observation. This illustrates the temporal problem; it does not establish that an advertising platform uses Beam or this update mechanism. Freshness is not finality Metrics can mature at different rates. Impressions and clicks may become reportable relatively quickly, spend may need reconciliation, and conversions depend on event delivery, matching and attribution. OpenAI's Ads reporting documentation describes distinct update schedules for these metrics. Source: OpenAI: Ads reporting documentation. A report collected five minutes ago can still contain provisional conversion data. An attribution window defines which outcomes qualify for credit after an interaction; it does not necessarily guarantee that all eligible records have arrived or become immutable. Claim finality only when the platform documents that guarantee. Later information has raised our count to 15. The next morning, it falls to 14. When one purchase becomes two events The retailer sends browser-side and server-side notifications for the same order. Treating them as independent purchases can count one business event twice. Correct counting therefore depends on identity. Messages are not purchases Retries create a similar problem. If a sender receives no acknowledgement, it cannot tell whether the notification was lost or processed. Retrying improves delivery but may produce a second copy. A stable business-event identifier can help recognise repeated submissions: purchase_id = O-1042 Two notifications with that identity may describe one purchase. A second purchase, O-1043, must remain distinct even if the customer, amount and approximate time match. Deduplicating by those attributes alone could erase legitimate activity. Meta's recommended browser/server deduplication method matches both event identifier and event name. Those rules belong to Meta's contract; they are not universal matching rules for advertising platforms. Source: Meta: Handling Duplicate Pixel and Conversions API Events. Why exactly-once processing is not enough A framework may replay an event after failure while committing its effect on managed state exactly once. Flink documents this guarantee through checkpoint recovery; end-to-end guarantees also depend on the sources and output systems. Source: Apache Flink: Fault tolerance. But two different event identifiers can describe the same purchase. Applying each exactly once still counts two conversions. Processing guarantees cannot repair an incorrect business identity. Three reconciliation problems therefore need different identities. Event deduplication recognises records for the same occurrence. Reporting-row reconciliation recognises the same aggregate group within one report definition. Snapshot reconciliation determines when a newer observation replaces an earlier one. Why our report falls from 15 to 14 Assume a duplicate purchase notification was initially counted and later removed: 15 − 1 = 14 This correction is hypothetical, not a claim about any provider's production deduplication schedule. A client collecting both snapshots must not add them. If they describe the same aggregate under the same definition, 14 is the newer observation. Preserve 15 for audit history if useful, but distinguish it from an additional fact to sum. Reconciliation requires the report definition, full aggregation key and observation identity; the latest value still need not be final. When the API returns only part of the answer Our analyst requests campaign performance. The client receives a first page and continuation token, then loses the connection while requesting page two. Its accepted rows can be valid while the requested report remains incomplete. This failure is independent of late source events. Pagination does not automatically provide a snapshot Pagination divides a result into retrievable pieces. A client follows continuation tokens until the API says no pages remain. Whether those pages form a consistent snapshot depends on the documented contract. Google Ads Search, for example, documents cached query results and page tokens; SearchStream returns results through a streaming response. Consistency within a cached retrieval does not make the metrics immutable across later queries. Sources: Google Ads API: Page through results, Search and SearchStream. Retries must preserve the original question A timeout alone may not reveal whether a request reached the server or its response was lost. A read-only retry may be appropriate under the API's limits and token rules, but it must preserve the original account, dates, dimensions and attribution configuration. Use bounded retries, backoff and explicit failure states. If a required page cannot be retrieved, retain accepted rows and mark collection incomplete. Pagination and partitioning solve different problems Pagination divides one query result; partitioning divides a task into smaller queries. A monthly report might use one query per day, each with its own pages. The collector must finish those pages and verify that its partitions cover the intended scope without unintended overlap. Every submitted query can succeed while a day that was never requested remains missing. Successful API calls alone cannot prove scope coverage. Explore Algorithms & data Recovery requires more than saving a cursor After a crash, a useful checkpoint identifies the original query, completed partitions, accepted pages and continuation state. Tokens remain usable only under the API's rules. If one expires or cannot be resumed safely, restart the affected partition and reconcile its replacement observations without double-counting. Two clocks, two kinds of completeness Scroll across to follow the diagram. A text explanation is available below. EVENT TIME PROCESSING TIME CLIENT RETRIEVAL · A SEPARATE OPERATION 21 Nov · 18:0022 Nov · 00:0009:0015:00 UTCACBACB Page 1Accepted rows Valid observations are retained. Page 2Request times out A required page is still missing. Collection stateRetrieval incomplete This can happen even when source data is mature. A, B and C use the purchase times in the article's table. The API-page failure is a separate hypothetical collection; time on the source timeline does not measure pagination progress. Read “Two clocks, two kinds of completeness” as text Both timelines use the same UTC scale. Purchase A happens on 21 November at 18:10 and is processed at 18:11. C happens at 19:05; B happens later, at 20:15. B is processed on 22 November at 11:40, before C at 13:20. Event order A, C, B becomes processing order A, B, C. The sloping lines show delay, not another purchase. Late eligible notifications can revise an earlier conversion count. Retrieving every page cannot force those source events to arrive or establish finality. Separately, a collector accepts page 1 but times out on page 2. That is incomplete retrieval, regardless of the source's maturity. Either problem can exist without the other. Four properties, not one status Validate a report against four questions: Property Question Retrieval completeness Did the client retrieve every required page and partition? Scope coverage Does the result cover the requested accounts, dates, dimensions and metrics? Data maturity Have the underlying metrics reached a suitable processing state for this use? Decision suitability Does the evidence support the intended interpretation or action? These properties are related, but none guarantees the others. If nine of ten pages contain £900 in compatible, non-overlapping spend rows, £900 is their subtotal, not a verified total for the request. Receiving the final page resolves that retrieval gap without establishing conversion finality or causal impact. Explore Software & production What the reported conversions actually mean The collector now holds the complete available report: 14 attributed conversions. Whether advertising caused 14 additional purchases is a different question. Attribution assigns credit Attribution rules determine which observed conversions receive credit for ad interactions. They may specify eligible clicks or impressions, windows, matching information, reporting dates and attribution models. A customer already planning to buy the grinder might see an ad, click and purchase. The purchase can qualify for attribution even if it would have happened anyway. The report cannot directly observe that alternative outcome. Incrementality requires a counterfactual The causal question is: how many purchases happened because of the advertising that would not otherwise have happened? A controlled experiment helps estimate the outcome without the campaign. Suppose eligible customers are randomly assigned to treatment and control groups. Treatment customers are eligible for the advertising intervention; control customers are withheld from it under the experiment's design. We compare their outcomes: Scroll across to compare all columns → Group Customers Purchases Treatment 10,000 120 Control 10,000 100 The purchase rates are 1.2% and 1.0%, a difference of 0.2 percentage points. Under appropriate randomisation and measurement assumptions, this difference helps estimate the intervention's incremental effect. It does not mean advertising caused all 120 treatment purchases or that the observed difference is the exact effect. Sampling uncertainty, interference and implementation failures matter. Google's Conversion Lift documentation provides a production example of treatment/control comparisons for advertising impact. Source: Google Ads: Conversion Lift. A complete report can still support the wrong conclusion Suppose attributed conversions rise by 20% after a budget increase. Seasonal demand, a price reduction, inventory or competing campaigns could explain the change. The report has not isolated the budget increase's causal effect. Attributed reporting can support monitoring and operational decisions under explicit assumptions. Claims about additional sales require evidence that addresses the causal question. An agent recommending budget changes must preserve that distinction. Explore Measurement & ML Building a report another system can safely use The retailer asks an agent: "Should we increase the coffee-grinder campaign budget tomorrow?" A successful reporting call does not establish that the evidence supports a recommendation. The reporting service needs to expose what it retrieved and the conditions under which the figures can be used. Make the guarantees explicit A proposed consumer-side evidence envelope can include: Scope: account, period, time zone, currency, dimensions and metric definitions. Collection: completed pages and partitions, failures and verified coverage. Maturity: collection time, source freshness and known revision limitations. Provenance: source API, query identity and observation identifier. Semantics: attribution settings, reporting grain and missing-value definitions. Limitations: uncertainty and unsupported conclusions. This is an application design, not an existing OpenAI Ads response schema. Its purpose is to make the report's properties machine-checkable. The same report can be acceptable for one use and rejected for another A report with all requested pages and correct scope can still contain provisional conversions. A dashboard may display it with a freshness warning, while a budget-change workflow requires more mature metrics, a longer comparison period and additional performance evidence. Suitability depends on the intended use. The boundary between evidence and action Scroll across to follow the diagram. A text explanation is available below. READ-ONLY REPORT · EVIDENCE VALIDATION ACTION WORKFLOW · SEPARATE AUTHORITY Report envelopeLatest observation: 14 Carry scope, coverage, maturity, provenance and limitations. Application checksValidate evidence Does this report cover the intended comparison and required metrics? Decision policyCheck suitability Enforce maturity rules, decision assumptions and proposal permission. If either check failsReturn the limitation or request more evidence Keep accepted observations. The agent cannot override a failed application check. RecommendationPropose a budget change State the exact campaign, change and supporting assumptions. ApprovalAuthorise that change An authorised person or policy approves the specific action. ExecutionSubmit the permitted change Use a separately authorised write operation. VerificationCheck platform state Confirm the budget reached its intended value; sales impact still needs evidence. A proposed application boundary. Passing the evidence checks permits a recommendation under policy; it does not itself grant approval, API write access or proof of incremental sales. Read “The boundary between evidence and action” as text The report envelope carries the latest observation of 14 attributed conversions together with scope, collection evidence, maturity, provenance, semantics and limitations. Application logic validates evidence and applies the workflow's decision policy before an agent can submit a recommendation. A missing requirement returns a limitation or a request for more evidence. If checks pass, the agent may recommend a specific budget change. An authorised person or policy must approve that action before a separately authorised write operation executes it. Verification checks that the intended platform state was reached. A confirmed budget change does not prove that sales improved or that any improvement was caused by advertising. An enforceable decision boundary Before an agent submits a budget-change proposal, a policy might require: Scope matching the campaign and comparison period. Every required page and partition collected. Available metrics meeting the workflow's maturity policy. A specified decision model with explicit assumptions. Permission to propose the specific action. Enforce these checks in application logic. A failed condition returns a limitation or requests more evidence. The agent cannot override the policy by producing a persuasive paragraph. Recommendation is not execution Keep four operations distinct: Recommendation: The agent proposes a specific budget change. Approval: An authorised person or policy approves it before execution, with human approval where required. Execution: A separately authorised operation submits the change. Verification: The system checks whether the intended platform state was reached. A proposal does not establish that the budget changed. A confirmed budget change does not establish that sales improved or that advertising caused the improvement. Explore AI engineering Test your understanding Apply the distinctions to three situations before opening the answers. Case A: The missing page Nine of ten pages contain £900 in spend. The final page repeatedly fails. Can the collector report £900 as total campaign spend? Read the answer Answer: No. It is the subtotal of compatible, non-overlapping received rows. A required page remains missing, so the complete requested total is unknown. Case B: The late conversion Every page arrives, but the platform documents that recent conversion metrics may change. Is the report complete? Read the answer Answer: Retrieval and scope may be complete while conversions remain provisional. Preserve both facts. Case C: The budget recommendation Attributed conversions rise by 20% after a budget increase. An agent recommends another increase because the first "caused more sales." What is missing? Read the answer Answer: Causal evidence. A recommendation may be defensible under an explicit operational policy, but attributed growth alone does not prove incremental sales. A causal claim needs stronger evidence, such as a well-designed experiment. What a trustworthy report actually guarantees Our 12 → 15 → 14 sequence exposes several independent guarantees: event identity determines what counts; processing determines when information arrives; report definitions determine what rows mean; and collection validation establishes what the client received. Measurement assumptions then constrain the conclusions. A useful report carries those boundaries forward. Keep accepted rows with missing coverage, provisional figures with their collection time and revision limits, and unavailable metrics as missing values. A null conversion count must not silently become zero, and an attributed count must not become a claim of incremental sales. This discipline applies to financial dashboards, marketplace analytics and operational monitoring as well as advertising. The result should make clear what is known, what may still change, and what the evidence permits us to do next. Can you use this report? Optional practice: compare five prepared outcomes from a separate fictional UK account. Open the examples to inspect complete, empty, partial, stale and rejected collections. Prepared examples · Fictional data The request in each example Get daily impressions, clicks, spend and credited conversions for campaigns in a fictional UK ad account on 1 and 2 November 2026. Time zone and currency London time, GBP Conversion credit 30 days after a click or one day after a view. Results use the date of the ad interaction. Open an example to see what came back and what you can do with it. Complete reportThe final batch arrived What came back Both batches arrived, giving you three rows. Each row covers one campaign and day. Impressions 2,300 Clicks 64 Spend £36.00 Credited conversions Total unavailable One row shows zero conversions and another has no conversion count. The spend total covers all the returned rows, but there isn’t enough information to add up conversions. What to do next Use the spend total for the requested period. Record when you collected it and check for later updates before using recent figures to make a decision. Empty reportThe request finished with zero rows What came back The first batch was empty and said there were no more batches. There are no totals to show. No rows matched the request. That gives you no spend or conversion figures to interpret. What to do next Check the account, dates and filters. If those are right, report “no rows returned” and keep the totals blank. Partial reportAnother batch is missing What came back The first batch returned two rows and a marker for the next batch. The next batch never arrived. Rows received 2 Spend in rows received £30.50 £30.50 is the subtotal for the rows you have. The spend for the full period is still unknown. What to do next Keep the original dates and filters and use the saved marker to retry the missing batch. If you can’t recover it, label the report partial and carry the gap into any summary. Stale reportAll batches arrived, but the figures are old What came back At a review on 5 November, the team still had a complete report collected on 3 November. They refreshed the same dates and received revised figures. Same reporting dates, two collection times Metric 3 Nov, 09:00 5 Nov, 09:00 Spend £36.00 £36.30 Credited conversions Unavailable 3 Receiving every batch tells you the collection finished. It doesn’t tell you whether the platform has since updated the figures. What to do next Refresh the same request before using the old copy. Use the newer figures for the same dates, and retain both collection times so readers can see what changed. Rejected requestThe requester lacked access What came back In this example, the reporting tool refused the request because the signed-in person didn’t have permission for the selected account. It returned no report. The tool stopped at its access check. There are no figures to interpret for that account. What to do next Check that you selected the right account and ask an account admin to confirm your access. Retry once the account or permission has been corrected. Try the collector and keep the evidence Optional implementation: the local reporting collector exercises pagination, bounded retries and partial results using separate fictional fixtures. Each invocation starts a fresh run. Durable checkpoints and live collection remain design work; samples need no advertiser account. For live requests, use the OpenAI Insights API reference. General Insights is paginated. Oversized dedicated conversion reports return HTTP 413 without rows or a cursor, requiring smaller entity lists or non-overlapping date ranges. OpenAI reporting limits Keep advertiser credentials on the server and enforce account access. The downloads below are illustrative application references.
